title: The Tortoise and the Rabbit
bodyHtml:
Malagasy is a language with 25 million speakers, most of them living in Madagascar. Even though Madagascar is in Africa, Malagasy belongs to the Austronesian language family, making it a relative of Indonesian, Hawaiian, and many other languages spoken throughout the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Below are some sentences in Malagasy along with their English translations.

A1. Fill in the blanks in the table:

Nitsiky ny bitro kely.The small rabbit smiled.
Mitsiky ny bitro kely.The small rabbit smiles.
Mitsiky ny bitro mainty.The black rabbit smiles.
Mihaona ny sokatra ny alika.The dog meets the tortoise.
Niaro ny bitro ny sokatra.The tortoise protected the rabbit.
The tortoise meets the dog.
Nitsiky ny sokatra mainty.

A2. Here are a few more Malagasy sentences. Fill in the blanks in this second table:

Nihaona ny vorona ity bitro lehibe ity.This large rabbit met the bird.
Miaro ny sokatra lehibe iny alika iny.That dog protects the large tortoise.
Miarahaba ity sahona maitso ity ny saka.The cat greets this green frog.
Niteny ity alika kely ity.This small dog spoke.
This small dog speaks.
Niaro ny saka ity bitro lehibe ity.
This green bird greeted that small frog.

hints.text: Compare the first two sentences of the first table. They differ by a single letter at the very start of the first word, and the English differs only in whether the action already happened. That tells you where tense is marked.

Now look at where the doer and the done-to sit. In each Malagasy sentence the verb comes first, and the two noun phrases after it are NOT in English order: the thing being acted on comes first and the actor comes last. Also notice that words like “small”, “black” and “green” follow their noun, while ny (“the”) comes before it, and “this”/“that” are marked twice, once before and once after the noun phrase.

Try building a sentence that is not asked for, such as “That black cat greets the bird.” Verb first: miarahaba (present, m-). Then the object “the bird”: ny vorona. Then the subject “that black cat”: the noun and its adjective sit inside the iny ... iny pair, giving iny saka mainty iny. Result: Miarahaba ny vorona iny saka mainty iny. Use the same recipe on the graded items, remembering to switch m- to n- for the past.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the tense marker

The first two rows of table A1 are almost identical:

  • Nitsiky ny bitro kely. = “The small rabbit smiled.”
  • Mitsiky ny bitro kely. = “The small rabbit smiles.”

Only the first letter of the verb changes. So m- at the start of a verb means present tense (“smiles”) and n- means past tense (“smiled”). Every verb in the problem follows this: mihaona “meets” / nihaona “met”, miaro “protects” / niaro “protected”, miteny “speaks” / niteny “spoke”, miarahaba “greets” / niarahaba “greeted”.

Step 2: build a vocabulary list

Lining the sentences up gives: sokatra tortoise, alika dog, bitro rabbit, vorona bird, saka cat, sahona frog; kely small, mainty black, lehibe large, maitso green; ny “the”, ity ... ity “this”, iny ... iny “that”.

Step 3: work out the word order

Look at Mihaona ny sokatra ny alika. = “The dog meets the tortoise.” The verb is first. Then comes ny sokatra “the tortoise”, which is the object (the one being met), and last comes ny alika “the dog”, the subject (the one doing the meeting). So Malagasy order here is Verb - Object - Subject, the mirror image of the English Subject - Verb - Object.

Inside a noun phrase: adjectives come after the noun (bitro kely = “rabbit small” = “small rabbit”). ny “the” comes before the noun. The demonstratives “this” and “that” are written twice, wrapping around the whole noun-plus-adjective group: ity alika kely ity = “this small dog”, iny alika iny = “that dog”.

Step 4: apply it

For an English sentence, first find the verb and choose m- or n- for its tense. Write that verb first. Then write the object noun phrase, then the subject noun phrase, each with its own determiner and with any adjective placed after its noun.

Example that is not graded: “The large tortoise met that dog.” Verb: past of “meet” = nihaona. Object “that dog” = iny alika iny. Subject “the large tortoise” = ny sokatra lehibe. Result: Nihaona iny alika iny ny sokatra lehibe.

Going the other way, from Malagasy to English, read the verb, then remember that the noun phrase directly after the verb is the object and the last one is the subject, so you have to swap them when you write the English.

Why this matters

Verb-Object-Subject order is rare among the world's languages, and Malagasy is one of the best-known examples. Notice also how it keeps a consistent habit: modifiers such as adjectives follow the word they describe, the opposite of English.
